title: Marlowe v. Tennant Logistics, Inc.
court: U.S. Court of Appeals, Fourteenth Circuit (fictional)
text: Plaintiff, a warehouse supervisor, alleged that her termination violated Title VII, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a), because her manager repeatedly remarked that women could not handle night-shift leadership. Applying the burden-shifting framework, we hold that a plaintiff may establish pretext by showing that the employer's stated reason for termination is unworthy of credence, without separate direct evidence of discriminatory animus. Discriminatory remarks by the decision-maker that relate to the challenged employment decision are probative of pretext and may not be dismissed as stray remarks. To the extent Okafor v. Bellweather Foods Corp., 641 F.3d 87, required 'pretext plus' evidence of disparate treatment, it is overruled. The summary judgment for the employer is reversed.

title: Okafor v. Bellweather Foods Corp.
court: U.S. Court of Appeals, Fourteenth Circuit (fictional)
text: An employee claiming disparate treatment under Title VII, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2, must offer more than evidence that the employer's explanation for his discharge is false. We hold that the plaintiff must also produce independent evidence that discrimination was the real reason for the adverse employment action. Isolated comments by supervisors about an employee's national origin are stray remarks that cannot by themselves defeat summary judgment. Because Okafor offered no evidence beyond his supervisor's remarks and the inconsistency in the employer's explanation, judgment for the employer is affirmed.

title: Delgado v. Summit Ridge Hospital
court: U.S. District Court, District of Ardmore (fictional)
text: A respiratory therapist with a chronic autoimmune disorder requested a modified schedule as a reasonable accommodation under the Americans with Disabilities Act, 42 U.S.C. § 12112(b)(5)(A). The hospital denied the request without meeting with her and terminated her for attendance violations. The regulations at 29 C.F.R. § 1630.2(o)(3) contemplate an informal, interactive process to identify the precise limitations resulting from the disability and potential accommodations. An employer that fails to engage in that process in good faith may be liable where a reasonable accommodation would have been possible. The hospital's motion for summary judgment is denied.

title: Haverford v. Pacific Crest Software, Inc.
text: Under the California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), an employer must engage in a timely, good faith interactive process with an employee who requests a reasonable accommodation for a known disability. We hold that the failure to engage in the interactive process is an independent violation of FEHA, actionable even if the employee cannot yet identify an accommodation that would have succeeded. The Act's definition of disability is broader than the federal standard, and courts should not import narrower federal limitations. Federal authority such as Delgado v. Summit Ridge Hospital, 944 F. Supp. 3d 512, is persuasive but does not limit the protections the Legislature enacted. The judgment of the Court of Appeal is reversed.

title: Nguyen v. Golden Valley Unified School District
text: A teacher alleged age discrimination under the Fair Employment and Housing Act after she was not rehired at age sixty-one. The district relied on the same-actor inference, noting that the principal who declined to rehire her had hired her three years earlier. We hold that the same-actor inference creates a strong presumption that the adverse employment decision was not discriminatory. Because the teacher offered only statistical evidence about the ages of new hires, summary judgment for the district is affirmed.

title: United States v. Calloway
text: Police arrested Calloway for a traffic offense and, without a warrant, searched the call logs, messages and photographs stored on his smartphone. The search incident to arrest exception to the Fourth Amendment rests on officer safety and the preservation of evidence, and neither rationale justifies a search of the digital data on a seized phone. A modern cell phone holds the privacies of life, and its contents differ in both quantity and quality from physical objects found on an arrestee. Officers must generally secure a warrant before searching the data on a cell phone seized incident to arrest. The contrary container analysis of United States v. Brandt, 588 F.3d 940, is rejected.

title: United States v. Brandt
court: U.S. Court of Appeals, Fourteenth Circuit (fictional)
text: Officers arrested Brandt on a drug distribution charge and read the text messages on the cell phone found in his pocket. We hold that a cell phone is a container like a wallet or address book, and that officers may search its contents without a warrant as a search incident to a lawful arrest. The Fourth Amendment does not require officers to distinguish between physical and digital containers carried on the arrestee's person. The motion to suppress the messages was properly denied.

title: United States v. Ostrowski
court: U.S. Court of Appeals, Fourteenth Circuit (fictional)
text: Investigators obtained a geofence warrant directing a technology company to disclose location history for every device within a two-block area during a robbery. Ostrowski moved to suppress, arguing that the warrant lacked particularity and probable cause as to each device. We hold that collecting historical location data is a Fourth Amendment search, consistent with the heightened protection for digital data recognized in United States v. Calloway, 731 U.S. 204. The warrant was overbroad, but the good-faith exception applies because the officers reasonably relied on a judicially issued warrant. The denial of suppression is affirmed.

title: United States v. Pemberton
court: U.S. Court of Appeals, Fourteenth Circuit (fictional)
text: A trooper stopped Pemberton's truck for speeding and smelled burnt marijuana through the open window. Under the automobile exception, officers may search a vehicle without a warrant when they have probable cause to believe it contains contraband. We hold that the odor of marijuana, together with the driver's inconsistent account of his travel, supplied probable cause to search the passenger compartment and the trunk. The search of the vehicle did not violate the Fourth Amendment, and the conviction is affirmed.

title: People v. Ashworth
text: After arresting the defendant for driving with a suspended license, officers impounded his car and conducted an inventory search that uncovered a handgun in a closed backpack. Under article I, section 12 of the New York Constitution, an inventory search of an impounded vehicle must follow a standardized departmental procedure designed to produce a meaningful inventory. Where officers record only selected items and the search is a pretext to look for evidence of crime, the vehicle search is unlawful and its fruits must be suppressed. People v. Kessler, 702 N.E.2d 1189, is overruled to the extent it tolerated investigatory inventory searches. The order denying suppression is reversed.

title: People v. Kessler
text: Police stopped the defendant's car for a broken taillight, impounded it, and found cocaine in the console during an inventory search. The defendant argued that the officers' true motive was to look for drugs. We hold that an inventory search of an impounded automobile is valid whenever the impoundment is lawful, regardless of the officers' subjective motivation. The suppression motion was properly denied.

title: Brightwater Capital LLC v. Sorensen
text: An investor opened an online brokerage account by clicking a button labeled 'Open Account' beneath a hyperlink to the platform's terms, which included an arbitration clause. Contract formation online, as elsewhere, requires an offer, an acceptance and mutual assent, which may be manifested by conduct. We hold that a clickwrap agreement is enforceable where the user receives reasonably conspicuous notice of the terms and takes an unambiguous action manifesting assent to them. A browsewrap notice buried at the bottom of a page, by contrast, does not bind a user who never saw it. Because the terms were presented directly above the button, the motion to compel arbitration is granted.

title: Lindqvist v. Harborview Marine Supply, Inc.
text: A boat dealer sent a written offer to sell two engines at a fixed price, and the buyer replied accepting but adding a new delivery term. Under the common law mirror image rule, an acceptance must comply exactly with the terms of the offer. A purported acceptance that adds or changes material terms is a counteroffer that rejects the original offer. Because the dealer never assented to the counteroffer, no contract was formed, and the complaint for breach of contract was properly dismissed.

title: Ramirez v. Sunfield Telecom, Inc.
text: A wireless customer sued over hidden fees, and the carrier sought to compel arbitration under terms posted on its website. The terms were reachable only through a small link at the bottom of the checkout page, and the customer was never asked to check a box or click to agree. We hold that a browsewrap agreement is unenforceable unless the consumer had actual or constructive notice of the terms. Mutual assent to an online contract turns on whether a reasonably prudent user would have been on inquiry notice. The order denying the motion to compel arbitration is affirmed.

title: Ashdown Holdings Ltd v. Pereira Engineering Ltd
text: The parties exchanged purchase orders and acknowledgments containing conflicting standard terms before the goods were delivered and accepted. Applying the traditional offer and acceptance analysis, the court held that each document was a counter-offer and that the contract was concluded on the last set of terms sent before performance. This 'last shot' approach gives commercial certainty in a battle of the forms. The judge was right to hold that the seller's limitation clause formed part of the contract, and the appeal is dismissed.

title: Fennimore v. Castlegate Borough Council
text: The claimant was injured when a dangerous tree on private land fell onto a public footpath, and she argued that the local authority owed her a duty of care because it had powers of inspection. The court held that the existence of a duty of care in negligence is determined by established principles and incremental development by analogy, not by applying a three-stage test of foreseeability, proximity and fairness as a universal formula. Public authorities are generally under no common law duty to confer a benefit by preventing harm caused by third parties or natural events, absent an assumption of responsibility or the creation of the danger. Trelawney v. Northgate Rail plc [2004] EWCA Civ 3390 is overruled in so far as it held otherwise. The appeal is allowed.

title: Trelawney v. Northgate Rail plc
text: A passenger was injured by a falling sign on a station platform and sued both the operator and the public regulator that had failed to enforce safety standards. The court applied the three-stage test, asking whether the harm was foreseeable, whether there was sufficient proximity and whether it was fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty of care. It held that the regulator owed a duty of care to passengers because injury resulting from its omission to act was plainly foreseeable. The appeal against the finding of negligence was dismissed.

title: Hollins v. Brackenridge Construction Ltd
text: The claimant purchased a house in reliance on a structural survey commissioned by the developer and suffered loss when defects in the foundations emerged. Recovery for pure economic loss in negligence requires an assumption of responsibility by the defendant towards the claimant. The court held that the surveyor knew the report would be passed to purchasers and relied upon without independent inquiry, so a duty of care in respect of negligent misstatement arose. Damages were awarded for the cost of remedial works.

title: Castellano v. Metropolitan Transit Authority
text: A commuter slipped on an icy stairway leading to a subway platform during an ongoing storm. A landowner owes a duty of reasonable care to maintain its property in a safe condition in view of all the circumstances, including the foreseeability of injury. Under the storm in progress doctrine, however, the duty to remove snow and ice is suspended until a reasonable time after the storm ends. Because the storm was ongoing, the authority was not negligent, and summary judgment dismissing the complaint is affirmed.

title: Vantage Pictures, Inc. v. Lumen Archive Project
court: U.S. Court of Appeals, Fourteenth Circuit (fictional)
text: A nonprofit archive digitized film stills and published them with critical commentary on the history of studio advertising. Fair use under 17 U.S.C. § 107 requires weighing the purpose and character of the use, the nature of the copyrighted work, the amount used, and the effect on the potential market. We hold that a use is transformative when it adds new expression, meaning or message rather than superseding the original, and that commercial character is only one consideration. Because the archive's commentary served a different purpose and there was no evidence of harm to a market for licensed stills, the use was fair. To the extent Sterling Music Group v. Echofield Media, Inc., 402 F.3d 616, treated commercial use as presumptively unfair, we decline to follow it.

title: Sterling Music Group v. Echofield Media, Inc.
court: U.S. Court of Appeals, Fourteenth Circuit (fictional)
text: A streaming service used thirty-second clips of popular recordings in advertisements for its subscription plans. We hold that every commercial use of copyrighted material is presumptively an unfair exploitation of the copyright owner's exclusive rights. The defendant failed to rebut the presumption because the clips served the same entertainment purpose as the original recordings. The fair use defense under 17 USC 107 therefore fails, and the injunction is affirmed.

title: In re Kestrel Analytics Consumer Privacy Litigation
text: Consumers alleged that a data broker sold their browsing histories and precise geolocation to advertisers without honoring their requests to opt out of the sale of personal information. Under the California consumer privacy statute, a business must give notice at collection and honor a consumer's request to opt out of the sale or sharing of personal information. The statute's private right of action, however, is limited to data breaches caused by a failure to maintain reasonable security procedures. Claims for unlawful sale of data must be enforced by public authorities, or pursued under the unfair competition law where the consumer suffered an independent economic injury. The demurrer to the statutory privacy claim was properly sustained, but the unfair competition claim may proceed.

title: Statutory summary: former California Online Data Disclosure Act
text: This summary describes the former California Online Data Disclosure Act, which required commercial websites collecting personal information from California residents to post a conspicuous privacy policy. The Act required disclosure of the categories of personal information collected and of the third parties with whom it was shared, but it gave consumers no right to opt out of the sale of their data. Enforcement was limited to actions under the unfair competition law after a thirty-day cure period. The disclosure provisions were superseded by the comprehensive consumer privacy statute, and this summary is retained for historical research only.

title: Pemberley v. Orbis Fitness Data Ltd
text: A fitness application operator shared its users' heart-rate and location data with insurers without a lawful basis. The claimant sued for misuse of private information and for compensation under the Data Protection Act 2018. The court held that health data attracts a reasonable expectation of privacy and that sharing it with insurers for commercial profiling was a misuse of private information. Compensation for a data protection contravention extends to non-material damage such as distress, but must be proved by each claimant individually. The appeal was allowed in part.
